extracted.intended_audience: children / young students learning natural history (elementary school)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical identification and basic natural-history knowledge of common insect orders and species, presented as an introductory textbook chapter for children. Emphasizes diagnostic features (wings, mouthparts, life history, behavior) and simple field/observational cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use grouping to aid memory
rubrics_metrics.description: If we can group together things that are like each other, it is easier to remember them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ORDER ORTHOPTERA is usefully subdivided into 'Running Orthoptera' (cockroaches), 'Grasping Orthoptera' (praying mantis), 'Walking Orthoptera' (walking sticks), and 'Jumping Orthoptera' (short-horned grasshoppers/locusts, long-horned meadow grasshoppers, crickets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Odonata wing diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: The wings of the Odonata are stiff and covered with a close network of fine veins, and all four of them are alike. No wing covers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish dragonflies/odonates from Orthoptera by wing venation and all four wings being similar in form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ephemerida (mayflies) wing diagnostic and name meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: May flies (Ephemerida) have hind wings that are quite small; the name comes from Greek 'ephemeros' meaning lasting but a day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small hind wings and ephemeral adult life as identifying features; young (larvæ) breathe with gills (see respiration entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plecoptera (stone-flies) hind-wing folding
rubrics_metrics.description: Stone flies have four wings but their hind wings are folded in plaits; hence called 'plaited wings' (Plecoptera).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for plaited/folded hind wings to separate Plecoptera from Odonata and Ephemerida.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thysanura (silverfish) wingless, bristle-tailed
rubrics_metrics.description: The little silver fish has no wings at all; its order is called Thysanura from its bristle tail ('thysanos' meaning tassel and 'oura' tail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of wings and presence of bristle tail identify Thysanura.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'bug' (Hemiptera) — life stage and mouthparts
rubrics_metrics.description: A bug has four wings—when it has any—but its wings are not like those of Orthoptera, Odonata, Ephemerida, or Plecoptera. Young bugs are like old bugs (only smaller) and have no wings. Bugs do not 'bite' (chew); they 'suck' with mouthparts often grown together into a tube (beak) used to pierce and suck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key hemipteran traits: piercing-sucking mouthparts (beak), hemimetabolous development (nymph resembles adult), and a characteristic wing arrangement in many species (see 'half-wing' entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hemiptera 'half-wing' (hemiptera) structure
rubrics_metrics.description: In many bugs the upper wings are half stiff like a wing cover and half thin and silky, folding the delicate underwing beneath; this upper-half/under-half arrangement characterizes many of the bug order—hence the name Hemiptera (half-wing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying bugs, check the upper wings for a stiff basal portion and a membranous apical portion; not all bugs have this, but many do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiracles and insect respiration (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insects have no lungs; they breathe through a row of holes or pores (spiracles) along each side of the abdomen (and some on the thorax). The spiracles open into air tubes that carry air to the blood of the insect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spiracles are often visible on the abdomen and in some caterpillars appear as bright-colored spots. Abdominal movements ventilate the tracheal system; observe abdomen movement to detect breathing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larval respiration exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some larvæ breathe by gills and do not have spiracles until they are grown up (e.g., larvæ of dragon flies and May flies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying aquatic insect larvae, look for gills rather than spiracles; adult respiration will be by spiracles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air layer and hydrophobic hairs (water-surface respiration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some aquatic insects (e.g., water boatman) are covered with fine hairs that entangle a layer of air around the body, making them appear silver under water and allowing them to carry an air supply to breathe while submerged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under magnification look for dense hydrophobic hairs; behaviorally, these insects may carry an air envelope and make swimming movements to renew it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water-boatman locomotory adaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: Water boatman's hind legs have a fringe of hairs and are modified to paddle—acting as oars for swimming; they cling by front feet and row with modified hind legs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hind-leg morphology (flattened, fringed with hairs) indicates swimming specialization; observe anchoring behavior and paddling motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aquatic insect seasonal behavior (hibernation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many aquatic insects bury themselves in mud at the bottom of ponds in winter and remain inactive (hibernation) until spring, surviving with very little air and taking no food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider overwintering strategies when searching for seasonal presence/absence in ponds; buried stages may persist without feeding for extended periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diet and feeding mode of water-boatmen and related bugs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many water bugs (e.g., water boatman) suck the juices of other insects; some species' eggs and bodies are used as food by people (e.g., in Mexico) or as feed for captive birds and fish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feeding mode (piercing-sucking) can be inferred from mouthparts; ecological notes (e.g., eggs glued to plants) inform life-cycle observations and possible human uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back-swimmer identification and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Back-swimmers are similar to water boatmen but have a keel-shaped back and often swim on their backs, using long paddles (hind legs); they have a sharp beak that can pierce and sting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe swimming posture (on back) and body shape (keel-like dorsum) plus defensive biting/stinging behavior to distinguish back-swimmers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giant water-bug morphology and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Giant water bugs are large, flat, brown, fly to lights at night (sometimes called electric light bugs), have fore legs that shut up like a jackknife with the tibia fitting into a groove in the femur (raptorial forelegs), can capture and suck blood of fish and other prey, and in some species males carry eggs glued to their backs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for large flat form, raptorial forelegs, nocturnal attraction to lights, and unusual parental care (male carries eggs) as diagnostic and behavioral traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing antennæ from legs (walking-sticks, threadlike forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some insects have long threadlike structures that may look like legs but are antennæ (or vice versa). Antennæ often lack little feet, whereas legs are jointed with feet; some walking-stick-like insects have front appendages folded and appear as threads until they move.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully observe jointing and presence/absence of tarsi (little feet) to determine whether an appendage is an antenna or a leg; watch movement patterns (antennae used as feelers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lace-bug feeding and egg-laying
rubrics_metrics.description: Lace bugs suck plant juices (do not eat other insects) and lay curious eggs glued fast to leaves that look like little out-growths of the leaf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microscopic/close inspection reveals lacy dorsal appearance and glued eggs on leaf surfaces; useful for identifying plant-sap-feeding Hemiptera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bed-bug diagnostic traits and biology
rubrics_metrics.description: Bed bugs are round, flat, reddish-brown, with a short sharp tube folded under the head (used to pierce skin and suck blood); they have no wings (only rudimentary scales), lay eggs in cracks and crevices (eggs likened to little jars with lids), young resemble adults, and can live a very long time without feeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect infestation by appearance, odor (disagreeable smell from defensive/other secretions), eggs in cracks, and persistence after vacancies; cleanliness and vigilance are recommended to prevent infestations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural pest traits: red bugs and chinch bugs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Hemiptera (red bugs, chinch bugs) pierce and suck juices of crops (e.g., cotton, grain, oranges), stain or kill plant tissue, reproduce quickly (e.g., two broods per year for chinch bugs), and can cause economic devastation if in large numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale of infestation (millions) determines severity; inspect for characteristic markings (e.g., white wing covers with black markings in chinch bugs) and seasonal brood timing for management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological control examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Pest control methods include introducing diseased insects into fields to spread contagion among pests, or introducing predatory insect species that prey upon injurious insects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives historical/examples: introducing diseased chinch bugs or beneficial predatory insects; note contagion and predator-host dynamics as ecologically based control strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stink-bug chemical defense and ecological role
rubrics_metrics.description: Stink bugs eject a disagreeable liquid from pores on the underside of the thorax when disturbed; such odors commonly serve to repel predators. Some stink-bug species are beneficial predators of other insects, while many feed on fruits and vegetables and can cause damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When handling or collecting, be aware of defensive secretions; observation of feeding habits distinguishes pest vs beneficial species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lice (true lice) parasitic morphology and hosts
rubrics_metrics.description: True lice are wingless parasites with claws and a sucking mouth tube; they cannot survive without a living host and include species infesting humans and animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate bird lice and book lice (which are not true lice and belong to other orders) by body form and taxonomy; parasitic lifestyle (claws, host specificity) is diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cicada morphology, song organs, and life cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicadas (sometimes called locusts) are Hemiptera with four similar glassy wings (no wing covers), a broad head and body, compound eyes plus three simple ocelli between them, male 'kettle-drum' song organs (tymbals) producing loud shrill calls, a sharp tube-like mouth for sucking plant juices, and a life cycle with nymphs that burrow and live underground (e.g., two years or up to 17 years), then climb and molt to adults. Females use an ovipositor to slit twigs and lay eggs; nymphs drop and burrow, feeding on roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify cicadas by wing form, tymbal structures (male), ocelli, and life-history clues (cast skins of chitin on trees, long subterranean nymphal periods). Cast skins are chitinous and may persist on vegetation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept of vestigial/survival organs in evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Some insect organs (e.g., ocelli) may be present in some species but not others; when an organ ceases to be used, it dwindles over evolutionary time and may disappear, being called a 'survival' of an ancestral organ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/absence of small structures (ocelli, rudimentary wings) as clues to evolutionary history and comparative anatomy, but be cautious about functional interpretation.
